lesson.title: Trusses: the method of joints

lead.text: A truss is a frame built from straight bars called members, joined at their ends by pins called joints. Loads are applied at the joints and nowhere else. The simplest truss is a single triangle. The load hangs from the top joint, which is called the apex. The two lower corners rest on supports.

A triangle is the building block because it cannot change shape unless a member gets longer or shorter. Push on the corner of a four-sided frame and it folds flat. Push on the corner of a triangle and the members simply resist. Bigger trusses are triangles added to triangles. The picture shows two small ones, each with a 20 kN load at the apex.

afterFigure.text: Because each member is so simple, a truss can carry a large load with very little material. The next screen looks at what each member feels.

lead.text: The load hangs from the middle, so nothing favours either foot.

The members are straight, joined by pins and loaded only at the joints, so each member is acted on only at its two ends. For the member to stay at rest, those two forces must be equal and opposite along its own line. Every member is simply pulled or pushed along its length. A member that is pulled, stretched like a rope, is in tension. A member that is pushed, squashed like a post, is in compression.

Hang a lamp from a rope and the rope is in tension. Stand a post under a floor and the post is in compression. Which one a member is depends on how it acts on the joints at its ends. If it pulls them towards each other it is in tension, and if it pushes them apart it is in compression. The difference matters because a long thin bar copes well with a pull and buckles under a push.

diagram.alt: One straight bar between two joints. In the first view the arrows on the joints point towards each other, which is tension. In the second the arrows point away from each other, which is compression.
diagram.caption: A bar that pulls its joints together is in tension. A bar that pushes them apart is in compression. Use the buttons to compare the two.

lead.text: Picture the rope and ask whether it is being stretched or squashed.

To find the force in a member, imagine cutting the frame apart at one joint and drawing that joint alone with every force on it, as in a free-body diagram. Start at the apex, since only three things act there: the load pulling down and the two sloping members. The truss is symmetrical, so the two sloping members carry equal forces, F.

From the first lesson, a member's upward share is its force times rise ÷ length. Take a truss with a span of 8 m and an apex 3 m high, so that each sloping member is 5 m long. A 30 kN load hangs from the apex. The two members together must hold up the load, so 2 × F × 3/5 = 30, which gives F = 25 kN.

afterFigure.text: That is more than the 15 kN half of the load, because a sloping member only gives 3/5 of its force upwards. The flatter the truss, the harder each sloping member works.

lead.text: Cut out the apex joint. Two equal members meet there and hold up the load between them.

steps.headline: A truss spans 6 m with its apex 4 m high, so each sloping member is 5 m long. A 24 kN load hangs at the apex. Find the force in each sloping member.

lead.text: Here is the same method on a taller truss, written out line by line.

workedSteps.text: At the apex two members share the load, each with vertical share rise over length.
The members push down and outward on the feet, so they are in compression. The bottom member pulls the feet together, so it is in tension.

lead.text: That settles the sloping members. Now move to the foot of the truss, joint A on the left support. In the 8 m truss a sloping member presses on it with 25 kN along the slope. Its sideways part is 25 × run ÷ length, which is 25 × 4/5 = 20 kN, directed outward along the ground.

Nothing loads the truss sideways, so the pin at A has no horizontal reaction. The only thing left to hold that foot still is the bottom member, which joins the two feet. It must supply 20 kN along the ground to balance the outward push. The force in the bottom member equals the horizontal part of the sloping member's force.

afterFigure.text: Whether the bottom member pushes or pulls on the foot is a separate question, and it decides whether the member is in tension or compression. The next questions come back to it.

steps.headline: At joint A of the 4 m truss with a 1.5 m high apex, AC pushes with 10 kN along a line with run 2 m and length 2.5 m. Find the force in AB, in kN.

lead.text: The bottom member balances the horizontal part of the push from AC.

workedSteps.text: Nothing loads the truss sideways, so the pin at A has no horizontal reaction.
AB must cancel the horizontal part of AC's push: its share is run over length, 2 ÷ 2.5.
Multiply AC's force by that share, in kN.

lead.text: Think about which way the bottom member must act on the foot to stop the sloping members spreading it.

steps.headline: A joint with nothing hanging from it

lead.text: Some members carry no force at all. Add a short vertical member DC that joins the middle of the bottom bar, joint D, to the apex. Look at joint D alone. Nothing hangs from it. The two bottom members meet at D along one straight, horizontal line. DC leaves it vertically.

Balance the vertical forces at D. The horizontal members have no vertical part, so DC is the only member with one. With no load and no other vertical force, DC's own vertical force must be zero. A member like this is called a zero-force member. It still has a use: hang the load from D instead of the apex and DC carries that load up to the apex.
Joint D has no load on it, and the two members along the bottom lie on one line.

lesson.orientation: Find member forces joint by joint and tell tension from compression.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Look up inside a barn roof or along the side of a railway bridge and you will see the same pattern repeated: straight bars joined at their ends to make triangles. Nobody puts a thick beam where thin bars will do, and the triangles are what make that possible. Each bar is only ever pulled or pushed along its own length.

Hang a heavy load from the tip of one triangle and every bar feels something. The two sloping bars press down on the feet and try to spread them apart. The bar along the bottom holds them together. Choosing the right size for each bar depends on knowing the force in it.
This lesson works out those forces for a small triangular frame. It uses the first three lessons: splitting a force into parts, sharing a load between supports and balancing forces.

diagram.alt: A triangular frame of three straight bars with a load hanging from the top joint. Two sloping bars rise to the load and a bar runs along the bottom between the two feet. Arrows show the feet being pushed outwards.
diagram.caption: The load presses the sloping bars down on the feet and pushes the feet outwards. The bar along the bottom has to hold them in.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the forces in a simple truss one joint at a time, and say whether each member is pulled or pushed.

recap.keyIdea: Isolate one joint with at most two unknown member forces and balance it. Each member is then a pure push or pull along its length.

blocks.text: Back at the small frame, you found 10 kN in each sloping member of a 4 m truss under 12 kN, and 8 kN pulling along the bottom bar. You also found that an unloaded joint with two members on one line leaves the third member with no force.

recap.nextHook: Now that you know the force in each bar, the next lesson asks how much force a bar of a given size can carry before it gives way.

questions.prompt: A symmetrical triangular truss carries a 12 kN load at its apex and rests on two supports, one under each foot. What force, in kN, does each support carry?
hints: The truss is symmetrical and the load is at the middle.
Together the two supports carry the whole load.
Divide the load between the two supports.
questions.onCorrect: 6 kN each. A symmetrical load is shared equally between the supports.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load on one support. The two supports share it.
Two supports do not double the load. Together they carry exactly the load.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The supports share the 12 kN load equally, so each carries 12 ÷ 2 = 6 kN.

questions.prompt: A rope holds up a hanging lamp. Is the rope in tension or compression?
hints: Is the rope being stretched or squashed?
questions.onCorrect: The rope is pulled along its length, so it is in tension. A member that is pushed is in compression.

misconceptions.feedback: Compression squashes a member. A rope that holds something up is being stretched.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tension. The rope is stretched along its length, so it is in tension.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss spans 4 m with its apex C 1.5 m above the supports, so each sloping member is 2.5 m long. A 12 kN load hangs from C. Find the size of the force in member AC in kN.
hints: Isolate joint C. Two equal member forces meet there.
Each contributes a vertical part of F × rise/length.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At C, both sloping members have vertical parts of F × 1.5/2.5. Then 2 × 0.6F = 12, so F = 10 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kN. Each member's vertical part is only 0.6 of its force, so the slanting members carry more than half the load each.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the second sloping member. Both share the load.
That is each member's vertical share. The member itself carries more, because it slants.

questions.prompt: Why is there a factor of 2 in 2 × F × 4/5 = 24?
hints: How many members meet at the apex joint?
questions.onCorrect: Each member that meets the joint adds its own vertical part, and two meet at the apex.

misconceptions.feedback: The load is counted once. The 2 counts the members meeting at the joint.
A member's vertical part is its force times rise over length, not double it.

choices.label: Two sloping members meet at the apex and each gives an equal vertical part.
The load is counted twice, once for each support.
Each member carries double its own vertical part.

acceptedIdeas: Two sloping members meet at the apex and each gives an equal vertical part.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two sloping members meet at the apex and each gives an equal vertical part.. Two members meet at the apex, each giving a vertical part of F × 4/5.

hints: AB cancels the horizontal part of AC's push.
That part is the force times run over length.
Calculate 10 × 2/2.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Horizontal balance at A: FAB = 10 × 2/2.5 = 8 kN, in tension.

questions.onCorrect: 8 kN. The bottom member balances only the horizontal part of the push of AC.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in AC, along the slope. AB balances only its horizontal part.
That is the vertical part. AB has to cancel the horizontal part.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss carries a load at its apex, and its two sloping members push outward on the feet. Is the bottom member AB, which joins the feet, in tension or compression?
hints: Picture the sloping members spreading under the load. What must AB do to stop the feet moving apart?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tension: AB pulls inward to stop the supports spreading apart.

questions.onCorrect: AB pulls the feet together: a member that pulls on its joints is in tension.

misconceptions.feedback: A member in compression pushes on its joints. AB has to stop the feet spreading, so think about which way it acts on them.

questions.prompt: A king-post truss adds a vertical member DC from the middle of the bottom chord, D, up to the apex C. The only load is 12 kN at C. Find the force in DC in kN.
hints: Isolate joint D and list the members meeting there.
AD and DB lie on one straight line; DC is the only member with a vertical part.
Write ΣFy = 0 at D with no load applied there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At D, AD and DB are collinear and horizontal and no load acts, so vertical balance leaves DC with no force.

questions.onCorrect: DC carries nothing: at an unloaded joint, only DC has a vertical part, so it must be zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the applied load, but it acts at C, not at D.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss spans 3 m with its apex 2 m high, so each sloping member is 2.5 m long. A 16 kN load acts at the apex. Find the tension in the bottom member in kN.
hints: Find the sloping member force first, at the apex.
Then use horizontal balance at a support joint.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the apex: 2F × 2/2.5 = 16, so F = 10 kN in each sloping member. At a support: tension = 10 × 1.5/2.5 = 6 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 6 kN. The apex gives the sloping force; the horizontal part of it is what the bottom member balances.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in each sloping member. The bottom member balances only the horizontal part.
That is the vertical part of a sloping member. The bottom member balances the horizontal part.

questions.prompt: A truss spans 6 m with its apex 4 m high, so each sloping member is 5 m long. A 32 kN load hangs at the apex. Find the force in each sloping member in kN.
hints: Isolate the apex joint.
Two members each give a vertical part of F × 4/5.
questions.onCorrect: 20 kN. Two members share the load, and each gives only 4/5 of its force upward.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load. Two members share it, and each is slanted.
That is each member's vertical share. The member itself carries more because it slants.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the apex 2F × 4/5 = 32, so F = 32 ÷ 1.6 = 20 kN.

questions.prompt: A member pushes outward on the joints at both its ends. What is it in: tension or compression?
hints: Ask whether the member is being stretched or squashed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compression: a strut pushes on its joints.

questions.onCorrect: A member that pushes on its joints is squashed: compression.

misconceptions.feedback: A member in tension pulls on its joints. This one pushes them.
